pages.x: In April 1978 Afghan communists seized power in a coup and set out to remake the country by force. They broke up estates, changed the rules of marriage, and arrested and killed thousands of opponents. Revolts spread through the countryside, and in March 1979 the city of Herat rose up. Soviet advisers were among the dead.

Moscow decided to step in. On 27 December 1979 Soviet special forces stormed the palace in Kabul, killed the president, Hafizullah Amin, a communist the Kremlin no longer trusted, and put Babrak Karmal in his place. Tens of thousands of troops rolled in over the border. The old men around Leonid Brezhnev thought it would all take a few months.

The Afghans who fought back called themselves mujahideen, those who wage jihad. They were farmers, tribesmen and village mullahs, split into many rival parties, and they fought from the mountains, ambushing convoys on the roads. Through Pakistan, the United States and Saudi Arabia sent them money and guns, and Arab volunteers came to join them.

In the Panjshir valley north of Kabul a young commander, Ahmad Shah Massoud, beat back one Soviet offensive after another, slipping away into the side valleys and striking again when the troops left. His men called him the Lion of Panjshir. Away from the cities and the main roads, the Soviets never really held the country.

Soviet aircraft bombed villages that sheltered the rebels, and millions of mines were laid in the fields. Between half a million and two million Afghans were killed, and whole valleys emptied as people fled to camps in Pakistan and Iran, the largest crowd of refugees in the world at the time.

In 1986 the United States began giving the mujahideen Stinger missiles, light enough to fire from the shoulder, which brought down Soviet helicopters and jets. Pilots had to fly higher, and lost much of their edge. Historians still argue about how much the missiles changed the war, but Moscow was already looking for a way out.

The new Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, called the war a bleeding wound. In 1988 he agreed to pull out, and on 15 February 1989 the last Soviet commander walked back across the bridge over the Amu Darya into the Soviet Union. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers had died, and many more came home wounded in body or mind.

The communist government held out for three more years, until Soviet aid stopped. Then the mujahideen leaders turned on each other, and their rockets reduced much of Kabul to rubble. In 1996 a new movement of religious students from the south, the Taliban, took the city.

The war drained the Soviet Union of money and of faith in its leaders, and helped bring it down. For Afghanistan it was the start of more than forty years of war. Some of the Arab volunteers who came to fight the Soviets, among them Osama bin Laden, went on to found al-Qaeda.
pts: The last Soviet soldiers left in February 1989
